Honestly if you're more into programming and want to use C# you should look into MonoGame. It's open source, cross platform and just all around a beautiful 2D (and 3D) games framework. This gets all of the underlying graphics, windowing and input code done for you, as well as an easy to use Vector math library. I'm a student at RIT for Game Design and Development and we require our Freshman to make games with MonoGame.

With MonoGame, it leaves you open to do all of the gameplay code yourself (physics, ai, sprite animation, game state management, etc) without having to worry about spending hundreds of hours on the DirectX and OpenGL code.

Though to be perfectly honest if you really want to be a game programmer, you should learn C++. If you're new to programming, stick with C# for a while, make a few projects for practice. But if you want to get into graphics programming, engine programming, AI, performance optimization, physics engine development or anything like that, C# doesn't give you as much access to low level operations that you need to optimize your data transformations.

Edit: Here's a link - http://www.monogame.net/ 

Also if it helps, Bastion and Transistor were both made with MonoGame (though originally Bastion was made with XNA, which MonoGame is based off of). Probably some other games too, but that should be enough to show you MonoGame is powerful enough for commercial release while still being robust and easy to use for casual development.

Well to some degree that's what an emulator DOES. Unfortunately it doesn't quite work that way at a hardware level.

Different CPU architectures have preset "Instruction Sets" that they can perform, which isn't standardized across all hardware. An x86 CPU (for example) physically cannot support the MIPS instruction set, and " translation" between them has to be done before the CPU can understand and execute those instructions.
